body:
Conventional urea and nano urea supply the same primary nutrient

Urea is a major nitrogenous fertiliser. Conventional agricultural urea is generally sold as solid granules or prills containing approximately 46% nitrogen by mass. Once applied to soil, it undergoes transformations that make nitrogen available for plant uptake. Its contribution is nitrogen nutrition; it is not a direct source of phosphorus or potassium.

Nano urea is a formulated nitrogen fertiliser designed for efficient nutrient delivery, commonly through foliar spraying. It supplies nitrogen, but its concentration, physical form and recommended application method differ from those of granular urea.

Different nano urea products have different nitrogen concentrations

The label nano urea does not indicate one universal nitrogen percentage. The Government of India has notified several nano nitrogen products under the Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985.

ProductReported nitrogen concentrationOfficial notification
IFFCO Nano Urea Plus16%15 April 2024
Zuari Farm Hub Nano Urea8%29 November 2023
Ray Nano Urea4.4%6 March 2023

These concentrations were reported by the Department of Fertilisers on 8 August 2025. The earlier IFFCO Nano Urea liquid specification also described a 4% nitrogen formulation. Therefore, older descriptions of Nano Urea Liquid should not be confused with the subsequently notified IFFCO Nano Urea Plus formulation containing 16% nitrogen.

Always identify the exact product. The original IFFCO nano urea formulation, IFFCO Nano Urea Plus and nano urea products made by other manufacturers should not be assigned the same concentration merely because their names contain nano urea.

How nano urea is intended to be used

Foliar nano urea is generally intended as part of a nutrient-management programme. The crop still needs adequate nitrogen at the appropriate growth stages, along with phosphorus, potassium and other essential nutrients.

Government field-trial findings reported on 20 March 2026 indicated that foliar nano urea, used together with the recommended basal dose of conventional fertilisers, achieved comparable yields in some trials while allowing a 25–50% reduction in conventional urea use. Reported yield gains in various crops ranged from 3–8% under the trial conditions.

These figures describe results from particular studies; they are not universal application recommendations or guaranteed outcomes for every field.

Why a small bottle does not automatically equal a bag of urea

A conventional fertiliser's nutrient concentration expresses how much nutrient it contains. For example, a 45 kg quantity of ordinary urea containing 46% nitrogen contains approximately 20.7 kg of nitrogen. A small bottle of nano urea contains a much smaller physical quantity of nitrogen.

Claims about reducing conventional urea requirements concern how effectively a product is used under specified agronomic conditions. They should not be interpreted as saying that a bottle and a bag contain equal amounts of nitrogen.

The Department of Fertilisers also acknowledged in its March 2026 report that some studies had identified inconsistent crop performance and nutrient deficiencies at higher substitution levels, including 50%, particularly in low-fertility soils. Long-term evaluations were therefore being undertaken.

Consequences for crop management

Applying nitrogen in excess of crop requirements can waste fertiliser and increase nutrient losses. Conversely, removing too much conventional nitrogen without adequate supplementary uptake can create a nitrogen shortage. Balanced decisions therefore depend on the crop, soil fertility, stage of growth and the exact product directions.

Nano urea cannot correct phosphorus deficiency, potassium deficiency or other nutrient shortages simply because its nitrogen delivery is efficient.

Prelims focus

  • Conventional urea contains approximately 46% nitrogen by mass.
  • IFFCO Nano Urea Plus containing 16% nitrogen was notified on 15 April 2024.
  • Other notified nano urea products have different nitrogen concentrations.
  • Government findings reported on 20 March 2026 concerned partial urea reduction with appropriate basal fertilisation.
  • Nano urea supplies nitrogen, not all primary nutrients.
  • Trap: Reported fertiliser savings do not mean that a nano urea bottle contains the same nitrogen mass as a conventional urea bag.

[Sources: Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Import and Sale of DAP, 8 August 2025, paragraph on notified nano nitrogen fertilisers, release 2154208; Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Government Highlights Significant Progress in Nano-Fertilizer Adoption and Drone-Led Agricultural Transformation, 20 March 2026, release 2242958; IFFCO, Nano Urea Plus (Liquid), product description and historical technical specification, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Basal fertilisation plus foliar nano urea led to mixed trial results; outcomes depend on soil, crop and nutrient balance, so substitution is conditional.
pictures.caption: Nano urea is assessed as a supplementary nitrogen strategy, not as an unconditional replacement.

title: Nano Urea: Nitrogen Supply, Product Grades and Scientific Limitations

body:
What is DAP?

DAP stands for diammonium phosphate, a manufactured fertiliser containing nitrogen and phosphorus. Its chemical formula is (NH4)2HPO4. The conventional granular product is widely identified by its grade 18-46-0.

This grade signifies 18% nitrogen, 46% phosphorus expressed as P2O5 equivalent and 0% potassium expressed as K2O equivalent. Conventional DAP is generally applied to soil before or during sowing so that phosphorus is available for early root development.

Why phosphorus matters during early growth

Phosphorus is involved in energy transfer and the formation of nucleic acids and cell membranes. It supports root development, cell division and normal crop establishment. Its availability depends partly on soil conditions because phosphorus can react with soil constituents and become less readily available to plants.

Phosphorus does not perform the same role as nitrogen. Adding more urea cannot directly correct a phosphorus shortage, just as adding DAP cannot by itself correct a potassium shortage.

What is Nano DAP Liquid?

Nano DAP Liquid is a formulated fertiliser intended to provide nitrogen and phosphorus through a nanoscale delivery system. The IFFCO product description specifies 8% nitrogen and 16% phosphorus expressed as P2O5, both on a weight-per-volume basis.

The same product description identifies particles smaller than 100 nm. It describes application through appropriate seed treatment and foliar methods, according to product directions.

Nano urea supplies nitrogen. Nano DAP supplies nitrogen and phosphorus. Neither product is a complete NPK fertiliser unless potassium is separately included in a specifically identified formulation.

Conventional DAP and Nano DAP are not interchangeable grades

FeatureConventional DAPIFFCO Nano DAP Liquid
Principal nutrientsNitrogen and phosphorusNitrogen and phosphorus
Reported composition18% N; 46% P2O58% N; 16% P2O5
Composition basisPercentage by mass for a solid productWeight per volume for the liquid product
Usual applicationSoil application, commonly basalSpecified seed-treatment and foliar methods
Potassium supplyNo declared KNo declared K

The percentages in the 2 products use different measurement bases. Consequently, their numerical grades should not be compared as though they represented equal package quantities or identical chemical formulations.

Where seed treatment and foliar feeding fit

A product authorised for seed treatment may be used before sowing to support early nutrient availability. Foliar application can later supply nutrients through leaves. These methods may complement soil fertilisation, but they do not automatically provide all the phosphorus a crop requires over its entire life cycle.

What field-trial findings establish

On 20 March 2026, the Department of Fertilisers reported that trials involving Nano DAP had shown comparable yields in certain cases when conventional phosphorus fertilisers were partially substituted using appropriate application methods. It cited substitution of up to 50% in some circumstances, including potato trials.

The phrase in certain cases is important. Soil phosphorus reserves, crop requirements and other nutrient inputs influence results. The findings do not establish that a fixed quantity of Nano DAP can replace the same proportion of conventional DAP everywhere.

Prelims focus

  • DAP stands for diammonium phosphate.
  • The conventional DAP grade is 18-46-0.
  • IFFCO Nano DAP Liquid is described as containing 8% N and 16% P2O5, on a weight-per-volume basis.
  • Conventional DAP is principally a soil-applied NP fertiliser.
  • Specified Nano DAP formulations may be used for seed treatment and foliar application.
  • Trap: Neither conventional DAP nor the described Nano DAP formulation supplies potassium.

[Sources: IFFCO, DAP 18-46-0, product and application sections, consulted 3 November 2026; IFFCO, Nano DAP (Liquid), product description and nutrient specification, consulted 3 November 2026; Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Government Highlights Significant Progress in Nano-Fertilizer Adoption and Drone-Led Agricultural Transformation, 20 March 2026, release 2242958.]

pictures.alt: Crop-stage timeline shows specified Nano DAP seed treatment and foliar spraying, conventional DAP basal soil application, and shared nitrogen and phosphorus supply.
pictures.caption: Nano DAP can be associated with seed and foliar nutrition at different crop stages.

title: Nano DAP and Conventional DAP: Composition, Uses and Differences

body:
What is a biofertiliser?

A biofertiliser is a preparation containing beneficial living microorganisms that improve the availability or supply of nutrients to plants. Such microorganisms may live in the soil, around roots, within plant tissues or in association with plant roots.

Unlike a bag of urea or DAP, a biofertiliser is not primarily a concentrated quantity of manufactured nitrogen or phosphorus. Its principal contribution is biological activity, such as fixing atmospheric nitrogen or making existing soil phosphorus more available.

Biological nitrogen fixation is the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds that living organisms can use, carried out by certain microorganisms.

Nitrogen-fixing biofertilisers

Rhizobium: symbiotic nitrogen fixation

Rhizobium is associated with the roots of leguminous plants such as pea, gram and beans. Compatible bacteria infect the roots and form specialised structures called root nodules.

Within a functioning nodule, the bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogen compounds. The host plant provides the bacteria with substances derived from photosynthesis and a suitable environment. Both partners benefit from the association.

Rhizobium inoculants are therefore particularly relevant to compatible leguminous crops. They are not a universal inoculant for every crop species, because effective nodulation depends on the plant and bacterial strain.

Azotobacter and Azospirillum

Azotobacter includes free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria that can function in soil without forming the characteristic legume root nodules.

Azospirillum includes nitrogen-fixing bacteria commonly associated with the root region of various grasses and cereals. Their relationship with the plant differs from the specialised Rhizobium-legume nodule association.

These organisms may support plant nutrition, but their effectiveness depends on suitable environmental and crop conditions.

Cyanobacteria in paddy fields

Cyanobacteria, traditionally called blue-green algae, include nitrogen-fixing organisms such as Anabaena and Nostoc. They are especially relevant to wetland rice cultivation.

The floating aquatic fern Azolla supports a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial partner commonly known as Anabaena in school-level descriptions. The association is used in rice-based nutrient management because the system can contribute biologically fixed nitrogen and organic matter.

Phosphorus-related biofertilisers

Phosphate-solubilising microorganisms

Some soil phosphorus occurs in forms that plant roots cannot readily absorb. Phosphate-solubilising bacteria (PSB) and certain fungi help convert some poorly soluble phosphorus compounds into more accessible forms.

These microbes do not create phosphorus from atmospheric nitrogen. Instead, they help make phosphorus already present in the soil or added materials more available to plants.

Mycorrhizae: beneficial root-fungus associations

A mycorrhiza is a beneficial association between a fungus and plant roots. Fungal filaments can extend beyond the immediate root surface, improving access to nutrients and water. Many mycorrhizal fungi are particularly important for phosphorus acquisition.

Members of the fungal genus Glomus form mycorrhizal associations. The fungus receives organic substances from the plant, while the plant benefits from nutrient acquisition. Such associations can also improve tolerance to certain stressful soil conditions, although the effects vary.

Biofertiliser, manure and biopesticide: a crucial distinction

InputMain naturePrincipal role
BiofertiliserBeneficial living microorganismsImproves nutrient availability or supply
Organic manureDecomposed organic materialAdds nutrients and organic matter
Mineral fertiliserConcentrated nutrient materialDirectly supplies specified nutrients
BiopesticideBiological pest-control agent or productControls pests or diseases

For example, Rhizobium is used for nitrogen fixation, whereas Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is primarily known for biological insect control. Both involve microorganisms, but their agricultural purposes differ. A microorganism should be classified according to the function for which it is being used.

Prelims focus

  • Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in association with compatible legume root nodules.
  • Azotobacter is a free-living nitrogen fixer.
  • Azospirillum is commonly associated with the root region of grasses and cereals.
  • Anabaena and Nostoc are nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
  • Glomus forms mycorrhizal associations that help plants acquire phosphorus.
  • Trap: Phosphate-solubilising microbes make existing phosphorus more available; they do not fix atmospheric phosphorus.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 10, Microbes in Human Welfare, section 10.6, Microbes as Biofertilisers; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections 2.3 and 2.6–2.7, pp. 21–27, 2018–19 reprint; Indian Council of Agricultural Research, educational material on beneficial agricultural microorganisms and biofertilisers, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Beneficial microorganisms contribute to nutrient cycling in agricultural fields.

title: Biofertilisers: Beneficial Microorganisms and Their Nutrient Functions
